hints.title: Translate the parameter into a vertical shift
hints.body: Changing c moves the line y=x+c up or down without changing its gradient. The other graph always has −1≤3sinx+2≤5. Each “some value” statement needs a suitable choice of c.
hints.recap: An existence claim can be proved by one valid witness value.
hints.pitfall: The three statements do not require the same witness value.
hints.pause: Sketch the sine curve with its heights at −π, −π/2, 0, π/2 and π.

recall.reminder: Distinguish an existence claim from a claim about every parameter value.

hints.title: Explore a descending branch
hints.body: Try an intercept between one and two; compare heights at zero, the positive sine maximum and the next sine zero.
hints.recap: Height comparisons plus monotonicity can locate crossings.
hints.pitfall: One crossing does not exclude additional crossings elsewhere.
hints.pause: Complete the positive-interval check, then inspect the negative side.

recall.reminder: Height comparisons plus monotonicity can locate crossings.

hints.title: Use an endpoint witness
hints.body: Choose the intercept so the line passes through (π,2). Check the negative side, the next half-period, and the tail beyond 2π separately.
hints.recap: The sine range can exclude whole intervals.
hints.pitfall: A local sketch alone cannot establish uniqueness on the full real line.
hints.pause: Find the intercept, prove the crossing counts and classify the existence claims.

recall.reminder: The sine range can exclude whole intervals.

solution:
Statement 1: take c=1. For 0≤x≤π/6, the curve is at least 2 while the line is below 2. From π/6 to π/2, the curve is at least 3.5 while the line is below 3. From π/2 to π the curve decreases from 5 to 2 and the line increases through those heights, giving exactly one crossing. On the negative side, the curve is above the line at −π but below it at −π/2, so another crossing lies between them.

Statements 2 and 3: take c=2−π. For 0≤x<π, the curve is at least 2 and the line is below 2; they meet at π. For x<0 the line is below 2−π<−1, the curve’s minimum. For π<x<2π the curve is at most 2 and the line exceeds 2. For x≥2π the line is at least 2+π>5, the curve’s maximum. Thus π is the only intersection anywhere.

All three statements hold. Answer H.
knowledgePattern: Exhibit different intercepts for existential sine-line intersection statements
